evaluated.name: Receivable Inventory Build Under Leverage
evaluated.expression: MUL(ZSCORE(WINSOR(NEG(RATIO(ADD(recch, invch), at)), 1)), RANK(RATIO(lt, at)))
evaluated.hypothesis: The accrual channel most exposed to manipulation is the build-up of receivables and inventory reported directly in the cash-flow statement; the market should penalize an extra dollar of such non-cash earnings much more steeply when the firm carries a heavy liability burden that it cannot service with paper profits.
evaluated.reasoning: Cash-flow-statement components (recch, invch enter with decrease-positive sign, hence NEG) give a cleaner accrual measure than the balance-sheet difference and avoid the merger/acquisition contamination in DELTA-based working capital. Centering the accrual leg with ZSCORE means a median-accrual firm scores zero at every leverage level, so the leverage rank only steepens the accrual slope rather than adding a standalone distress tilt.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Depreciation Shading By Levered Firms
evaluated.expression: MUL(ZSCORE(WINSOR(NEG(DELTA(RATIO(dp, sale), 1)), 1)), RANK(RATIO(lt, at)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Extending asset lives or slowing write-offs lowers the depreciation-to-sales rate and inflates reported earnings without any cash consequence; this discretionary lever is most likely to be pulled, and most likely to precede impairments, at highly levered firms defending covenants.
evaluated.reasoning: Depreciation is a non-current accrual and an entirely different manipulation channel from working-capital accruals, so it tests whether the distress interaction generalizes beyond receivables and inventory. The ZSCORE-centered change ensures the leverage rank modulates the slope on depreciation shading rather than contributing a standalone leverage effect.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Payables Stretch Sign Flip
evaluated.expression: MUL(ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(apalch, at), 1)), ZSCORE(WINSOR(NEG(RATIO(re, at)), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: The payables component of accruals changes economic meaning with financial condition: for healthy firms a shrinking payables balance is a classic positive accrual that predicts poor returns, while for firms with an accumulated earnings deficit a swelling payables balance is involuntary supplier financing that precedes credit tightening and negative news.
evaluated.reasoning: Both legs are now demeaned, so the product is the pure interaction term and carries no standalone loading on the low-retained-earnings distress effect the critic identified. The sign convention is internally coherent precisely because apalch enters cash flow with the opposite sign to an accrual: the (low apalch, healthy) quadrant is the high-accrual Sloan case and the (high apalch, deficit) quadrant is the supplier-stretch case, and both are predicted to underperform.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Cumulative Accrual Overhang In Chronically Weak Firms
evaluated.expression: MUL(ZSCORE(WINSOR(TS_SUM(NEG(RATIO(ADD(recch, invch), at)), 3), 1)), RANK(NEG(MA(RATIO(pi, at), 3))))
evaluated.hypothesis: A single year of working-capital accruals is noisy, but three consecutive years of unreversed receivable and inventory build create an overhang of soft assets whose eventual write-down is most damaging for firms with chronically weak pretax profitability, which lack the earnings cushion to absorb it.
evaluated.reasoning: Replacing the loss-year mask with a cumulative accrual state and a continuously ranked chronic-profitability weight removes the large point mass at zero that would have made quantile sorts degenerate, so the long-short spread is a broad cross-sectional bet rather than a thin loss-firm subsample. The accrual leg is demeaned so the distress leg only steepens the accrual slope, and the multi-year accumulation plus multi-year profitability state is a distinguishable reversal-timing hypothesis rather than the documented one-year loss-firm accrual result.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Opaque Other Accruals In Fragile Firms
evaluated.expression: MUL(ZSCORE(WINSOR(ABS(RATIO(aoloch, at)), 1)), RANK(SUMRANK(RATIO(lt, at), NEG(RATIO(re, at)))))
evaluated.hypothesis: The residual "other operating assets and liabilities" bucket of the cash-flow statement is the least transparent accrual line, containing reserves, provisions and accrued liabilities; a large absolute movement there signals low earnings transparency, and opacity is punished with delayed price discovery mainly when the firm is also financially fragile.
evaluated.reasoning: This abandons the ambiguous taxes-payable construct entirely, replacing a variable whose rise usually just reflects higher profitability with a direction-free opacity measure that has no mechanical profitability interpretation. The opacity leg is demeaned so the ranked distress composite modulates the opacity slope instead of reintroducing the standalone distress return effect.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Illiquid Accrual Mix Under Leverage
evaluated.expression: MUL(ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(recch, invch), at), 1)), RANK(RATIO(lt, at)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Holding total working-capital accruals roughly fixed, their composition matters for levered firms: inventory build is illiquid, obsolescence-prone and poor collateral, whereas receivables can be factored or securitized, so a mix tilted toward inventory accruals is far more dangerous when debt must be serviced.
evaluated.reasoning: The leg SUB(recch, invch) is positive exactly when the inventory build exceeds the receivable build, isolating the composition dimension that is close to orthogonal to the accrual level tested elsewhere in the archive, rather than restating inventory growth relative to sales as in the Abarbanell-Bushee or Thomas-Zhang signals. Demeaning the composition leg leaves the leverage rank acting purely as a slope modulator, and the hypothesis is a collateral-liquidity mechanism that neither accrual level nor leverage identifies alone.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Accruals While Leverage Is Rising
evaluated.expression: MUL(ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(DELTA(ADD(SUB(wcap, che), dlc), 1), dp), at), 1)), RANK(DELTA(RATIO(lt, at), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Distress is a trajectory, not just a level: soft accrual-based earnings reported in the same year that the liability-to-asset ratio is climbing indicate a firm funding working-capital expansion with new debt, and it is this dynamic combination — not static leverage — that precedes forced reversal and write-downs.
evaluated.reasoning: Conditioning on the change in leverage rather than its level tests a deterioration mechanism that is only weakly correlated with the static leverage rank used elsewhere in the archive, so it teaches a distinguishable lesson about which distress state matters. Stable high-leverage utilities and REITs, which contaminate level-based conditioning, receive no weight here unless their balance sheets are actually worsening.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Accruals Against Rollover Pressure
evaluated.expression: MUL(ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(DELTA(ADD(SUB(wcap, che), dlc), 1), dp), at), 1)), RANK(RATIO(dlc, lt)))
evaluated.hypothesis: What makes accruals dangerous is near-term cash need rather than total indebtedness: a firm whose debt is concentrated in current maturities must convert receivables and inventory into cash within months, so accrual-heavy earnings at such firms are the least likely to survive contact with the refinancing calendar.
evaluated.reasoning: The short-term share of total debt is close to orthogonal to the leverage level, so pairing it with the same centered accrual leg as signal 1 isolates exactly which dimension of distress amplifies accrual mispricing — a maturity-structure lesson the archive has not yet tested. It also matches the economic story's emphasis on liquidity pressure rather than solvency.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Debt Financed Accrual Build
evaluated.expression: MIN(ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(DELTA(ADD(SUB(wcap, che), dlc), 1), dp), at), 1)), ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(DELTA(ADD(dlc, dltt), 1), at), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: The dangerous case is not accruals as such but accruals that had to be funded externally: a firm whose receivables and inventory swell while it simultaneously raises new short- and long-term debt is converting borrowed cash into soft assets, and that combination precedes both accrual reversal and rising default risk.
evaluated.reasoning: MIN of two demeaned legs is a conjunction, not a monotone reweighting of the accrual leg, so a firm with large accruals but no new borrowing (or large borrowing but no accrual build) is not flagged — this is exactly what the published Sloan sort cannot express and it is what the critic asked for. The short leg is symmetric and economically clean: firms generating cash while retiring debt, which is the survivorship profile the accrual-distress story predicts should outperform.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Low Depreciation Rate Versus Peers Under Leverage
evaluated.expression: MUL(IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(NEG(RATIO(dp, LAG(at, 1))), 1)), RANK(RATIO(lt, at)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Within an industry, a firm charging unusually little depreciation against its beginning-of-year asset base is assuming longer useful lives and understating the cost of capacity, inflating current earnings; levered firms have the covenant incentive to make that choice and the highest subsequent impairment risk.
evaluated.reasoning: Replacing the growth difference with an industry-demeaned level removes the direct loading on asset growth that made the previous version a proxy for the investment anomaly already spanned by CMA, and deflating by lagged assets means current-year capital spending does not mechanically depress the ratio. Putting dp in the numerator rather than in a growth rate also eliminates the instability for small-depreciation firms that the critic flagged.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Accrual Spike Against Own History In Fragile Firms
evaluated.expression: MUL(ZSCORE(TS_RANK(RATIO(SUB(DELTA(ADD(SUB(wcap, che), dlc), 1), dp), at), 5)), RANK(SUMRANK(RATIO(lt, at), NEG(RATIO(re, at)))))
evaluated.hypothesis: An accrual that is extreme relative to the firm's own five-year history is a far stronger manipulation flag than an accrual that is merely large in the cross-section, because it controls for the firm's stable business model; such a self-referential spike should be most reversal-prone at firms with high leverage and accumulated deficits.
evaluated.reasoning: This restores the mispricing sign rather than fitting the single generation-1 alpha, so it is an independent test rather than reverse-engineering, while still exploiting time-series information about accrual behavior. TS_RANK measures position in the firm's own distribution instead of volatility, which sidesteps the contested accrual-quality risk premium and produces a bounded, outlier-resistant accrual leg that is demeaned before the distress rank modulates its slope.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Accrual Build Per Dollar Of Equity Cushion
evaluated.expression: WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(DELTA(ADD(SUB(wcap, che), dlc), 1), dp), MAX(ceq, che)), 1)
evaluated.hypothesis: The economically relevant scale for an accrual is the loss-absorbing capital that must absorb its reversal, not total assets: the same dollar of soft working-capital growth is trivial for a firm with a thick book equity cushion and existential for a thinly capitalized one, so deflating by the cushion embeds distress directly in the measurement.
evaluated.reasoning: This replaces the cosmetic industry-neutral variant with a genuinely different functional form — distress enters as a deflator that is decreasing in fragility, which is the direction the generation-0 liability-deflator error got backwards — allowing us to learn whether cushion-scaling dominates multiplicative conditioning. Flooring the denominator at cash keeps it positive for near-zero or negative book equity firms, and 1% winsorization controls the thin-cushion tail while retaining the broad coverage of balance-sheet inputs.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Accruals Against Cash Adjusted Rollover Pressure
evaluated.expression: MUL(ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(DELTA(ADD(SUB(wcap, che), dlc), 1), dp), at), 1)), RANK(SUMRANK(RATIO(dlc, lt), NEG(RATIO(che, lct)))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Rollover pressure only bites when the firm cannot self-fund the maturing claim, so the conditioning state should combine a short-maturity debt structure with a thin cash buffer relative to current obligations; accruals booked by firms scoring high on both are the least likely to survive the refinancing calendar.
evaluated.reasoning: This is a targeted sharpening of the archive's best signal: it keeps the accrual leg identical so any change in performance is attributable to adding the cash-coverage dimension to the maturity dimension. A firm with 80% short-term debt but a large cash pile is not liquidity-constrained, and the current conditioner cannot tell it apart from a cash-poor one.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Soft Asset Build Under Rollover Pressure
evaluated.expression: MUL(ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(DELTA(SUB(act, che), 1), dp), at), 1)), RANK(RATIO(dlc, lt)))
evaluated.hypothesis: The reversal-prone element of accruals is the growth of non-cash current assets — receivables and inventory the firm must eventually convert to cash — and it is this asset-side softness, not the working-capital netting of liabilities, that becomes dangerous when debt is maturing.
evaluated.reasoning: The critic correctly noted that Δdlc appears inside the standard accrual numerator, so part of the rollover result could be a mechanical debt-structure effect; this version removes all debt terms from the accrual leg while holding the conditioner fixed, making it a clean attribution test. If the effect survives, the mechanism is genuinely about soft assets meeting short-dated liabilities rather than about debt appearing twice.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Soft Assets Funded By Maturing Debt
evaluated.expression: MIN(ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(DELTA(SUB(act, che), 1), dp), at), 1)), ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(DELTA(dlc, 1), lt), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: A firm that expands receivables and inventory while simultaneously increasing its short-dated borrowings has created an explicit maturity mismatch — illiquid soft assets financed by claims that come due within a year — and this specific funding pattern, not accruals or borrowing alone, forecasts distress-driven underperformance.
evaluated.reasoning: The MIN conjunction requires both conditions simultaneously and is not a monotone reweighting of either leg, and the earlier MIN construction with total debt issuance already produced a significant alpha (t = −2.04), so restricting the funding leg to short-maturity debt tests whether maturity is the active ingredient. The accrual leg excludes debt entirely, so the two legs share no mechanical component.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Operating Liability Stretch Under Rollover Pressure
evaluated.expression: MUL(ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(DELTA(SUB(SUB(lct, dlc), txp), 1), at), 1)), RANK(RATIO(dlc, lt)))
evaluated.hypothesis: A rapid build in non-debt, non-tax current liabilities — trade payables and accrued expenses — is conventionally a negative accrual and good news, but for firms already facing maturing debt it is involuntary financing from suppliers and employees that precedes credit withdrawal and operating disruption.
evaluated.reasoning: This revives the payables sign-flip idea whose generation-1 test pointed the right way (FF5 t = −1.69) but was crippled by 6% coverage from cash-flow-statement data, rebuilding it from balance-sheet current liabilities net of debt and taxes. It is the liability-side counterpart to signal 2, so the pair tells us which side of working capital carries the distress interaction.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Three Year Soft Asset Overhang Meets Refinancing
evaluated.expression: MUL(ZSCORE(WINSOR(TS_SUM(RATIO(SUB(DELTA(SUB(act, che), 1), dp), at), 3), 1)), RANK(SUMRANK(RATIO(dlc, lt), NEG(RATIO(che, lct)))))
evaluated.hypothesis: What must be liquidated when debt comes due is the accumulated stock of soft assets, not a single year's flow; three years of uninterrupted, undepreciated working-capital build creates an overhang whose forced unwinding is triggered precisely when short-dated debt and a thin cash buffer force the firm to raise cash from its balance sheet.
evaluated.reasoning: This abandons the equity-cushion deflator entirely, so it cannot be a microcap scaling artifact, and it changes the accrual leg from a one-year flow to a multi-year stock while holding the liquidity conditioner fixed — a stock-versus-flow lesson the archive has not yet learned on high-coverage data. The earlier cumulative test failed only on 8%-coverage cash-flow lines and with a profitability rather than a liquidity conditioner, so this is a substantively different test rather than a rerun.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Near Term Funding Gap In Revenue Months
evaluated.expression: WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(ADD(dlc, SUB(DELTA(SUB(act, che), 1), dp)), che), sale), 1)
evaluated.hypothesis: Accruals and distress can be expressed in the same units — dollars of cash the firm must find — so the economically primitive quantity is maturing debt plus the incremental cash absorbed by soft working capital (net of the depreciation shield) less the cash already on hand, measured against annual revenue; firms with a large gap must either refinance, liquidate soft assets at a discount, or issue equity.
evaluated.reasoning: This replaces the diagnostic product with an additive, units-consistent funding-requirement construct in which the two themes are not multiplied but summed as competing claims on the same cash, a functional form absent from the archive. Deflating by sales rather than by book equity avoids the near-zero-denominator microcap distortion the critic identified in the cushion ratio while keeping a stable, broadly reported scale.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Funding Gap Net Of Internal Cash Generation
evaluated.expression: RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(ADD(dlc, SUB(DELTA(SUB(act, che), 1), dp)), ADD(che, oancf)), sale), 1))
evaluated.hypothesis: A firm facing maturing debt and a working-capital drain is only in trouble if operations cannot fund it, so subtracting operating cash flow alongside the cash stock converts the gap from a balance-sheet snapshot into a true external-financing requirement.
evaluated.reasoning: This isolates one design choice against signal 1 — whether internal cash generation belongs in the sources term — and it is exactly the variable that separates a growing, self-funding firm with high accruals from a fragile one that must go to the capital markets. It also sharpens the accrual interpretation, because a firm whose reported earnings are accrual-driven will show a large gap precisely when oancf fails to cover the claim.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Widening Funding Gap
evaluated.expression: RANK(WINSOR(DELTA(RATIO(SUB(ADD(dlc, SUB(DELTA(SUB(act, che), 1), dp)), che), sale), 1), 1))
evaluated.hypothesis: Markets price the level of a liquidity shortfall slowly but may miss its deterioration entirely; a gap that widened over the past year identifies firms whose accrual absorption and refinancing needs are growing faster than their revenue base, which is the state that precedes covenant breach and dilutive issuance.
evaluated.reasoning: Level versus change is a genuine and unresolved lesson in this archive — conditioning on rising leverage worked (alpha −2.8%, t = −3.24) while the level of leverage worked less well — and here it is tested on the construct with the strongest portfolio evidence. A change specification also purges persistent firm characteristics such as capital intensity and industry turnover that the level ratio inevitably carries.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Unbacked Earnings Meeting A Funding Gap
evaluated.expression: MIN(ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(ib, oancf), at), 1)), ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(ADD(dlc, SUB(DELTA(SUB(act, che), 1), dp)), che), sale), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: The most dangerous firm is the one whose reported profit is not backed by cash *and* which must find cash within the year; either condition alone is survivable, but their conjunction means the accounting story and the funding reality are about to collide.
evaluated.reasoning: MIN of two demeaned legs flags only firms failing both tests and is not a monotone reweighting of either, and the earlier MIN construction already delivered a significant alpha, so this tests whether pairing the funding gap with a pure earnings-quality measure adds to the gap alone. The two legs use different accounting primitives — income versus cash flow on one side, balance-sheet claims on the other — so there is no mechanical overlap driving the conjunction.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Accrual Turbulence Under Rollover Pressure
evaluated.expression: MUL(ZSCORE(WINSOR(ABS(RATIO(SUB(DELTA(ADD(SUB(wcap, che), dlc), 1), dp), at)), 1)), RANK(RATIO(dlc, lt)))
evaluated.hypothesis: For a firm with debt coming due, any large swing in working capital is a warning — an unusual build means cash is trapped in soft assets, while an unusual liquidation means the firm is already harvesting receivables and inventory to make payments — so the magnitude of the accrual, regardless of direction, should predict underperformance under liquidity pressure.
evaluated.reasoning: Every archive signal assumes a monotone accrual effect, yet the distress mechanism implies a non-monotone one: forced working-capital liquidation by a constrained firm is bad news even though it registers as a large negative accrual. Testing the absolute value against the same conditioner as the archive's best signal cleanly identifies whether the relation is one-sided or U-shaped, which determines how the whole family should be built from here.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Funding Gap Extreme Versus Peers And Own History
evaluated.expression: SUMRANK(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(ADD(dlc, SUB(DELTA(SUB(act, che), 1), dp)), che), sale), 1), TS_RANK(RATIO(SUB(ADD(dlc, SUB(DELTA(SUB(act, che), 1), dp)), che), sale), 5))
evaluated.hypothesis: A firm is genuinely in trouble when its near-term cash requirement is high both relative to other firms and relative to the way it has financed itself for the past five years; structurally gap-heavy business models are priced, but a firm sitting at the top of its own five-year gap distribution is experiencing a new and unpriced deterioration.
evaluated.reasoning: This is not a monotone re-expression of the archived gap: adding the firm's own time-series position materially reorders the cross-section, demoting low-turnover firms that always carry a large gap and promoting firms whose accrual absorption and maturing debt have just spiked. It also directly addresses the suspicion that the sale-deflated gap's alpha comes from a persistent business-model tilt rather than from a distress event, because the second leg is purely within-firm.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Accruals While Creditors Shorten The Leash
evaluated.expression: MUL(ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(DELTA(ADD(SUB(wcap, che), dlc), 1), dp), at), 1)), RANK(NEG(DELTA(RATIO(dltt, lt), 1))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Distress is revealed by the credit supply side: when the long-term share of a firm's liabilities falls, lenders are refusing to term out its debt, and accrual-heavy earnings reported in the same year are precisely the earnings that cannot be validated with cash before the shortened obligations come due.
evaluated.reasoning: This replaces the static maturity-structure level with a credit-rationing event — the change in the long-term debt share — which is a different economic object: dlc/lt describes how a firm is financed, while a falling dltt/lt says lenders have just changed their willingness to fund it. It therefore reweights an entirely different set of firms than the three archived dlc/lt variants, including levered firms with stable short-term financing that the level conditioner always flags.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Corrected Funding Gap With Cash Earnings
evaluated.expression: WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(ADD(dlc, DELTA(SUB(act, che), 1)), ADD(che, ADD(pi, dp))), sale), 1)
evaluated.hypothesis: The near-term cash requirement is maturing debt plus the working capital the firm must fund, and the resources against it are cash on hand plus pretax income added back for depreciation — the standard non-cash charge — so a firm whose soft-asset absorption and debt maturities exceed its cash earnings must go outside for money.
evaluated.reasoning: This fixes a genuine accounting defect in the archive's best signal, where depreciation was netted against a change in *current* assets, an operation with no economic meaning; moving dp to the sources side as a non-cash add-back makes the construct an internally consistent cash-requirement identity. Using pretax income plus depreciation rather than oancf keeps coverage at balance-sheet/income-statement levels (the oancf version cost a third of the sample, dropping coverage to 0.071) and avoids the partial cancellation the critic noted, since oancf already embeds the working-capital change in the numerator.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Chronic Funding Gap
evaluated.expression: RANK(MA(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(ADD(dlc, SUB(DELTA(SUB(act, che), 1), dp)), che), sale), 1), 3))
evaluated.hypothesis: A one-year funding gap can reflect a lumpy investment or a single maturity; a gap sustained for three consecutive years identifies a business model that chronically consumes more cash than it generates and is therefore permanently dependent on refinancing at the market's discretion.
evaluated.reasoning: Averaging suppresses the year-specific measurement noise that likely flattens the gap's cross-sectional slope while retaining the persistent component that should drive a genuine distress premium, so it targets the fmb-versus-alpha disagreement with an economic rather than a cosmetic fix. It contrasts directly with the archived one-year level and one-year change, completing the level/change/persistence triple on the family's most successful construct.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Cash Needed While Lenders Shorten Maturity
evaluated.expression: MIN(ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(ADD(dlc, SUB(DELTA(SUB(act, che), 1), dp)), che), sale), 1)), ZSCORE(WINSOR(NEG(DELTA(RATIO(dltt, lt), 1)), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: A funding gap is only fatal if the credit market will not refinance it, so the firms to avoid are those that simultaneously need outside cash and are watching their lenders shift them out of long-dated into short-dated debt — demand for financing meeting a contraction in its supply.
evaluated.reasoning: The two legs come from independent data channels — a cash-requirement computation versus the maturity composition lenders impose — so unlike the archived MIN with ib−oancf there is no shared working-capital component to make attribution ambiguous. The credit-supply leg already produced a strong standalone slope (fmb = −2.84) while the gap produced the strongest alpha, and the conjunction demands both, which is exactly the state the economic story describes.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Liquidity Coverage After Accrual Absorption
evaluated.expression: WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(ADD(che, ADD(pi, dp)), DELTA(SUB(act, che), 1)), lct), 1)
evaluated.hypothesis: Express the accruals-distress state as a coverage ratio rather than a shortfall: cash on hand plus cash earnings, net of the cash swallowed by growth in soft working capital, measured against the obligations actually coming due; firms whose remaining coverage is high can absorb accrual reversals, and firms whose coverage is thin cannot.
evaluated.reasoning: This is a different functional form and a different sign convention from every archived signal — a bounded coverage multiple deflated by the claim base (lct is strictly positive and economically the right scale) rather than a shortfall deflated by a size proxy, which changes the cross-sectional shape that has been suppressing Fama-MacBeth slopes in the gap family. The accrual term enters as a drain on the numerator rather than as an additive requirement, so the construct rewards firms whose earnings arrive in cash and penalizes those whose earnings are absorbed by receivables and inventory.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Soft Assets Growing As Equity Erodes
evaluated.expression: MUL(ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(DELTA(SUB(act, che), 1), dp), at), 1)), RANK(NEG(GROWTH(ceq, 1))))
evaluated.hypothesis: A firm that is expanding receivables and inventory while its book equity is shrinking is consuming its loss-absorbing capital at the same time as it is increasing the pool of assets exposed to write-down, which is the classic pre-impairment configuration and the state in which auditors and lenders force recognition.
evaluated.reasoning: Equity erosion is a distress dimension the archive has never tested — every conditioner so far has been debt-side (leverage level, leverage change, maturity structure, credit supply) whereas this is the capital-account side, and shrinking ceq captures losses, buybacks-under-stress and write-offs that no liability ratio reveals. Because the conditioner is a growth rate of equity rather than a debt ratio, it reweights a different set of firms, including unlevered firms whose fragility is entirely earnings-driven.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Properly Netted Working Capital Accrual Under Liquidity Pressure
evaluated.expression: MUL(ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(DELTA(SUB(act, che), 1), DELTA(SUB(SUB(lct, dlc), txp), 1)), at), 1)), RANK(SUMRANK(RATIO(dlc, lt), NEG(RATIO(che, lct)))))
evaluated.hypothesis: The accrual that must be financed is the growth in non-cash current assets net of the growth in genuine operating liabilities — supplier and accrued-expense credit, excluding both debt and taxes payable — and it is this net financing requirement, not a depreciation-contaminated proxy, that becomes dangerous when short-dated debt and a thin cash buffer force asset conversion.
evaluated.reasoning: Every product-family signal in the archive nets fixed-asset depreciation against a current-asset change, an operation the critic correctly called economically meaningless, and separately the archive showed that dropping the liability side entirely destroyed the alpha; this specification keeps both sides of working capital and removes dp, so it identifies whether the family's power came from the correct accrual concept or from the mis-netting. Excluding taxes payable from the operating-liability side is deliberate, since tax deferrals reflect profitability and statutory timing rather than trade credit and were shown in generation 3 to carry the opposite sign.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Debt Shortfall Meeting Working Capital Absorption
evaluated.expression: MIN(ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(dlc, ADD(pi, dp)), sale), 1)), ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(DELTA(SUB(act, che), 1), sale), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: The additive gap treats a dollar of maturing debt and a dollar of working-capital absorption as interchangeable, but the distress story says they must coincide: a firm whose cash earnings already fall short of its maturing debt and which is simultaneously pouring cash into receivables and inventory has no way to close the shortfall internally.
evaluated.reasoning: This decomposes the archive's best construct into its two economic pillars and requires both rather than summing them, which is a genuinely different functional form that will flag a different, smaller and more extreme set of firms than the additive gap. It also cleanly separates the two themes across legs — distress in the first, accruals in the second — so a strong result is unambiguously an interaction rather than a re-weighted single-theme effect.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Cash Requirement Without Retained Earnings Fallback
evaluated.expression: MUL(ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(ADD(dlc, DELTA(SUB(act, che), 1)), ADD(che, ADD(pi, dp))), sale), 1)), RANK(NEG(RATIO(re, at))))
evaluated.hypothesis: A cash shortfall is survivable for a firm with a deep stock of accumulated profits and lethal for one financed entirely by external capital, because the latter must return to markets on the market's terms; accumulated retained earnings are the fallback that determines whether a funding gap becomes a distress event.
evaluated.reasoning: Every conditioner tested on the accrual leg has been a flow or maturity variable, and retained earnings — the cumulative internal-capital stock — has never been paired with the funding-gap construct even though it is the classic Altman fragility term. Centering the gap leg keeps the retained-earnings rank as a pure slope modulator, so this asks whether the gap's −5.5% alpha is concentrated in firms with no earned-capital cushion.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Ranked Conjunction Of Cash Need And Credit Withdrawal
evaluated.expression: MIN(RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(ADD(dlc, SUB(DELTA(SUB(act, che), 1), dp)), che), sale), 1)), RANK(NEG(DELTA(RATIO(dltt, lt), 1))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Financing demand meeting a contraction in financing supply is the sharpest distress state available in accounting data: the firm needs outside cash and its lenders are simultaneously refusing to term out its obligations.
evaluated.reasoning: The z-score version of this conjunction produced a significant alpha (−2.3%, t = −2.27) but a wrong-signed Fama-MacBeth slope (+1.01), which is the diagnostic signature of MIN being applied to two legs with very different scales and tail shapes so that one leg dominates the minimum almost everywhere. Taking the minimum of two uniform ranks makes the conjunction scale-free and genuinely symmetric, which should repair the cross-sectional slope while preserving the economically distinct credit-supply channel.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Full Near Term Claim Stack Versus Cash Earnings
evaluated.expression: WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(ADD(lct, DELTA(SUB(act, che), 1)), ADD(che, ADD(pi, dp))), sale), 1)
evaluated.hypothesis: Trade payables and accrued expenses are claims that come due within the year exactly like maturing debt, so the economically complete near-term claim stack is total current liabilities rather than short-term debt alone, and a firm whose cash earnings and cash balance cannot cover the whole stack plus its working-capital growth is the one that must refinance or liquidate.
evaluated.reasoning: The archive has only ever used dlc as the near-term claim, yet generation 3 showed that operating-liability growth carries the *opposite* sign to debt growth, so widening the claim base is a genuine and non-obvious test of whether all near-term claims are equivalent or whether financial claims are uniquely dangerous. If the broader stack performs worse, that pins the mechanism specifically on debt-market refinancing risk rather than on generic liquidity, which sharpens the interpretation of the whole family.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Fragility Score With Accrual Absorption Component
evaluated.expression: SUMRANK(RATIO(SUB(DELTA(SUB(act, che), 1), DELTA(SUB(SUB(lct, dlc), txp), 1)), at), SUMRANK(RATIO(dlc, lt), NEG(RATIO(re, at))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Distress scoring in the Altman-Ohlson tradition uses leverage and earned capital but ignores earnings quality entirely; a firm whose net working-capital absorption is high, whose debt is short-dated, and which has no accumulated retained earnings is fragile in three complementary ways, and accrual quality belongs inside the score as a component rather than as an external conditioner.
evaluated.reasoning: This is built from three raw accounting channels rather than from any archived expression, so it is not a rank-ensemble of previously evaluated signals, and its economic claim — that accrual absorption is a distress *ingredient*, not a distress-conditioned effect — is a structurally different proposition from everything in the archive. Ranking each channel before summing produces the bounded, well-behaved regressor the gap family has lacked, which targets the persistent Fama-MacBeth weakness while keeping three independent sources of return signal in the extreme deciles.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Cash Requirement As Credit Supply Contracts
evaluated.expression: MUL(ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(ADD(dlc, DELTA(SUB(act, che), 1)), ADD(che, ADD(pi, dp))), sale), 1)), RANK(NEG(DELTA(RATIO(dltt, lt), 1))))
evaluated.hypothesis: A funding gap is priced correctly when lenders remain willing to term out debt and is mispriced when they are withdrawing; a falling long-term share of liabilities reveals a supply-side judgment about the firm that the market has not yet impounded into equity prices.
evaluated.reasoning: Both conjunctive tests of this demand-meets-supply idea failed on the cross-section (fmb +1.01 and +0.71) because MIN lets one leg bind almost everywhere, yet the credit-supply leg has the strongest standalone slope of any conditioner in the archive (−2.84); the multiplicative slope-steepening form is the specification that has repeatedly delivered both metrics. This keeps a genuinely distinct economic channel alive — lender behavior rather than firm balance-sheet stocks — in the functional form the evidence says works.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Cash Requirement With Weak Debt Coverage
evaluated.expression: MUL(ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(ADD(dlc, DELTA(SUB(act, che), 1)), ADD(che, ADD(pi, dp))), sale), 1)), RANK(NEG(RATIO(ni, ADD(dlc, dltt)))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Credit markets do not judge fragility by asset-scaled leverage but by how many years of earnings it would take to retire the debt, so the state that turns an accrual-driven cash requirement into a distress event is a low earnings-to-total-debt multiple, which is exactly the covenant metric lenders actually write.
evaluated.reasoning: Every distress conditioner tested in this archive scales claims by assets, retained earnings or liability composition; none has used the earnings-coverage multiple that determines refinancing terms in practice, and firms with negative earnings automatically land at the fragile extreme with the correct ordering under NEG. Because the conditioner is denominated in debt rather than assets, it reweights asset-light firms with modest book leverage but no earnings — a group every asset-scaled ratio in the archive treats as safe.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Cash Requirement With Understated Depreciation
evaluated.expression: MUL(ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(ADD(dlc, DELTA(SUB(act, che), 1)), ADD(che, ADD(pi, dp))), sale), 1)), RANK(NEG(RATIO(dp, LAG(at, 1)))))
evaluated.hypothesis: A firm that must find cash and is simultaneously charging unusually little depreciation against its opening asset base is flattering the very cash-earnings figure that appears in its funding calculation, so its reported shortfall understates the true one and its assets carry unrecognized impairment.
evaluated.reasoning: Every conditioner in the archive is a balance-sheet or lender-behaviour state; this is the first that conditions on an *accounting choice*, asking whether the funding gap is most mispriced where the accounting inputs to it are themselves least conservative. It also rehabilitates the depreciation channel, which failed as a standalone leg (alpha −0.1%) but was never tested as a modifier of a construct that already works.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Quick Coverage After Net Accrual Absorption
evaluated.expression: WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(ADD(che, ADD(pi, dp)), SUB(DELTA(SUB(act, che), 1), DELTA(SUB(SUB(lct, dlc), txp), 1))), SUB(lt, dltt)), 1)
evaluated.hypothesis: The resources genuinely available to meet claims coming due are cash plus cash earnings minus the cash swallowed by net working-capital growth, and the claims are every liability that is not long-dated; a firm whose earnings arrive in cash covers this stack comfortably while one whose earnings are absorbed by receivables and inventory does not.
evaluated.reasoning: The critic correctly noted that including act in the numerator made the accrual haircut second-order; removing the current-asset stock entirely leaves a numerator in which the net accrual term is the same order of magnitude as cash earnings, so earnings quality genuinely drives the ratio. The archived coverage ratio built this way against current liabilities produced +5.5% alpha with t = +4.58, and this version adds the properly netted accrual (assets less operating liabilities, excluding taxes) and the complete non-long-term claim base.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Cash Requirement With Illiquid Asset Base
evaluated.expression: MUL(ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(ADD(dlc, DELTA(SUB(act, che), 1)), ADD(che, ADD(pi, dp))), sale), 1)), RANK(NEG(RATIO(act, at))))
evaluated.hypothesis: A firm facing a cash shortfall has one internal escape route — shrinking its own balance sheet — and that route is open only if its assets are current; a fixed-asset-heavy firm cannot liquidate its way out within the year and must go to lenders or shareholders on their terms.
evaluated.reasoning: Every conditioning variable tried so far sits on the right-hand side of the balance sheet — leverage, maturity, earned capital, lender behaviour — whereas this asks whether the asset side determines the severity of the same shortfall, which is a genuinely different economic question about self-help capacity. It is also close to orthogonal to the archive's conditioners, since capital-intensive firms are not systematically the ones with retained-earnings deficits or short-dated debt.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Cash Requirement Alongside Below The Line Charges
evaluated.expression: MUL(ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(ADD(dlc, DELTA(SUB(act, che), 1)), ADD(che, ADD(pi, dp))), sale), 1)), RANK(NEG(RATIO(SUB(ni, ib), at))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Discontinued operations, extraordinary items and other below-the-line charges are the accounting footprint of a restructuring already underway; a firm taking such charges while also running a cash shortfall is one where write-downs have begun but the working-capital overhang has not yet been cleared.
evaluated.reasoning: The difference between net income and income before extraordinary items is a distress marker that no signal in the archive has touched, and unlike chronic-loss indicators it is continuous and does not create a point mass, addressing the defect the critic identified in the previous version. It also captures a distinct timing state — the market may already know the firm is restructuring yet still misprice the unresolved accrual absorption sitting on its balance sheet.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Uniformized Coverage Without Earned Cushion
evaluated.expression: MUL(ZSCORE(RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(ADD(che, ADD(pi, dp)), DELTA(SUB(act, che), 1)), lct), 1))), RANK(NEG(RATIO(re, at))))
evaluated.hypothesis: The mirror construct — cash and cash earnings surviving working-capital absorption, measured against obligations coming due — should reward firms whose earnings arrive in cash, and that reward should be largest for firms with no accumulated profits, because for them the coverage ratio is the only buffer that exists.
evaluated.reasoning: The unconditioned coverage ratio produced +5.5% alpha (t = +4.58) with a slope of only +1.77, exactly mirroring the gap family's imbalance, so applying the same two fixes — uniformization plus fragility conditioning — tests whether the diagnosis generalizes across a construct with a different deflator and the opposite sign. Confirming the mechanism on the mirror image is much stronger evidence than another variant on the same side of the ledger.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Cash Requirement Net Of Trade Credit
evaluated.expression: WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(ADD(dlc, SUB(DELTA(SUB(act, che), 1), DELTA(SUB(SUB(lct, dlc), txp), 1))), ADD(che, ADD(pi, dp))), sale), 1)
evaluated.hypothesis: Suppliers finance part of the working-capital build, so the cash a firm must actually raise is the growth in non-cash current assets *less* the growth in trade payables and accrued expenses; only the unfinanced residual represents a genuine external requirement.
evaluated.reasoning: Every version of this construct so far has counted the gross asset-side build as a cash need while the archive separately showed that operating-liability growth predicts *higher* returns, which is direct evidence that trade credit belongs on the sources side rather than being ignored. This is a change to what the signal measures rather than to how it is scaled or conditioned, and it should sharpen the identification of firms whose absorption is genuinely unfunded.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Abnormal Maturity Wall With Accrual Absorption
evaluated.expression: WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(ADD(SUB(dlc, MA(dlc, 3)), DELTA(SUB(act, che), 1)), ADD(che, ADD(pi, dp))), sale), 1)
evaluated.hypothesis: Firms with permanently high short-term debt run revolvers they roll as a matter of course, so the refinancing risk that matters is the *abnormal* portion of maturing debt relative to the firm's own recent norm, colliding with a working-capital drain and thin cash earnings.
evaluated.reasoning: Using the level of dlc treats a stable revolver borrower identically to a firm facing an unusual maturity wall, which plausibly dilutes the distress content of the requirement and contributes to the family's modest Sharpe ratios. Subtracting the firm's own three-year average of short-term debt keeps the accrual and cash-earnings terms as levels — they are genuinely current-period flows — while making only the debt term a deviation, which is the term whose level is a business-model constant.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Cash Requirement With Unpredictable Cash Earnings
evaluated.expression: MUL(ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(ADD(dlc, DELTA(SUB(act, che), 1)), ADD(che, ADD(pi, dp))), sale), 1)), RANK(VOL(RATIO(ADD(pi, dp), at), 5)))
evaluated.hypothesis: A cash shortfall is manageable when the resources that will close it are predictable and dangerous when they are not: firms whose cash earnings swing violently cannot plan around a maturity, cannot credibly commit to lenders, and are exactly the firms whose working-capital estimates are least reliable.
evaluated.reasoning: Every conditioner tested so far is a first-moment state — a leverage ratio, an earned-capital stock, a lender action, an asset mix — whereas this conditions on the second moment of the firm's cash-generating capacity, which is a distinct economic property that no balance-sheet ratio reveals and which is precisely what makes a funding requirement uninsurable. It also connects the two themes through uncertainty rather than through level fragility: volatile cash earnings imply volatile accruals, so the same conditioner rationalizes both the earnings-quality and the refinancing side of the story.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Absorption Rank Minus Cash Earnings Rank
evaluated.expression: SUB(RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(DELTA(SUB(act, che), 1), sale), 1)), RANK(WINSOR(RATIO(ADD(pi, dp), sale), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: The accruals-distress interaction can be expressed without any division as the distance between how aggressively a firm is absorbing cash into receivables and inventory and how strongly it is generating cash earnings; firms far up the absorption distribution and far down the cash-generation distribution are the fragile, low-quality-earnings cases.
evaluated.reasoning: This preserves the intensity idea the critic rejected while eliminating the denominator entirely, so there is no near-zero-scale artifact and no non-monotonicity — both legs are separately winsorized, sales-deflated and ranked before differencing. It is also a functional form the archive has never used: a signed rank spread, which is naturally bounded, symmetric and well behaved in a Fama-MacBeth regression, addressing the metric that has plateaued without relying on a monotone rescaling of an existing signal.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Cash Requirement At An Own History Liquidity Low
evaluated.expression: MUL(ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(ADD(dlc, DELTA(SUB(act, che), 1)), ADD(che, ADD(pi, dp))), sale), 1)), RANK(NEG(TS_RANK(RATIO(che, lct), 5))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Firms differ permanently in how much cash they hold, so the informative distress state is not the level of the cash buffer but whether the firm has drawn it down to the bottom of its own five-year range — a firm at its own liquidity low facing an accrual-driven cash requirement has already spent its reserves.
evaluated.reasoning: Every liquidity conditioner in the archive is cross-sectional (che/lct, dlc/lt), which confounds cash-rich business models with genuinely stressed firms; a within-firm position measure removes that permanent heterogeneity and isolates depletion, which is the economically active state. This is a different conditioning variable rather than a rescaling of an existing one, and because it is bounded in [0,1] by construction it cannot reintroduce the outlier problem that limits the family's cross-sectional slope.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Rank Space Funding Identity
evaluated.expression: SUMRANK(RATIO(DELTA(SUB(act, che), 1), sale), SUMRANK(RATIO(dlc, sale), NEG(RATIO(ADD(pi, dp), sale))))
evaluated.hypothesis: The cash-requirement identity — working-capital absorption plus maturing debt less cash earnings — is economically meaningful as an ordering of firms on each component, not as a dollar sum, so ranking the three terms separately before combining retains the full economics while removing the dominance of whichever term happens to be numerically largest.
evaluated.reasoning: The dollar-denominated identity yields alphas near −5.5% but slopes capped at −2.3, while the two-component rank spread yields a slope of −2.54 with no alpha, which localizes the problem precisely: rank space fixes the regression but the two-term spread discards the maturing-debt dimension that carries the portfolio payoff. This restores that third component in the same bounded space, which is the one specification the archive has never run and the only construction consistent with both diagnoses.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Cash Requirement While Revenue Contracts
evaluated.expression: MUL(ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(ADD(dlc, DELTA(SUB(act, che), 1)), ADD(che, ADD(pi, dp))), sale), 1)), RANK(NEG(GROWTH(sale, 1))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Working capital that expands while revenue shrinks cannot be justified by growth: the receivables were extended to buyers who are not returning and the inventory is not selling, so a cash requirement arising in a contracting business is the configuration in which the accrual will be written down rather than collected.
evaluated.reasoning: Every conditioner tested is a balance-sheet, lender, accounting-policy or cash-flow-moment variable; the demand environment in which the absorption occurred has never been used, even though it is the variable that determines whether soft assets convert to cash or to write-offs. Because the gap leg is demeaned and the conditioner bounded, this reweights growth-consistent absorption toward zero and concentrates the signal on firms whose accruals have no revenue justification.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Accelerating Working Capital Intensity Under Refinancing Pressure
evaluated.expression: MUL(ZSCORE(WINSOR(ACCEL(RATIO(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(SUB(lct, dlc), txp)), sale)), 1)), RANK(SUMRANK(RATIO(dlc, lt), NEG(RATIO(che, lct)))))
evaluated.hypothesis: A firm whose net working capital per dollar of revenue is not merely rising but rising at an increasing rate has lost control of its collection and inventory cycle, and that loss of control turns into a solvency problem when short-dated debt and a thin cash buffer force conversion on the firm's creditors' schedule rather than its own.
evaluated.reasoning: Every accrual leg in the archive is a level or a first difference; acceleration is a distinct economic state — deterioration that is itself worsening — and it identifies firms whose working-capital problem is compounding rather than one-off, which no level or change specification separates. Expressing it as intensity per unit of revenue and netting trade credit means the leg measures operating discipline rather than scale, and the liquidity conditioner supplies the distress channel that determines whether the compounding is survivable.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Deterioration From Own Best Cash Position
evaluated.expression: WINSOR(SUB(RATIO(SUB(ADD(dlc, DELTA(SUB(act, che), 1)), ADD(che, ADD(pi, dp))), sale), TS_MIN(RATIO(SUB(ADD(dlc, DELTA(SUB(act, che), 1)), ADD(che, ADD(pi, dp))), sale), 5)), 1)
evaluated.hypothesis: Each firm has demonstrated, at some point in the last five years, the tightest cash requirement its business model can achieve; the distance between today's requirement and that demonstrated best is a measure of how far the firm has drifted from its own attainable discipline, and drift of that kind is neither a business-model constant nor priced.
evaluated.reasoning: This uses a distance-from-extreme construction that the archive has never tested — the smoothing, first-difference and time-series-rank variants all measure something else, and unlike an ordinal position it retains cardinal information about how large the deterioration is. Because the benchmark is the firm's own historical minimum, capital intensity, margin and sector turnover are differenced out without any industry adjustment, which addresses the standing concern that the sales-deflated requirement embeds a business-model tilt.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Near Term Claim Intensity Including Committed Working Capital
evaluated.expression: WINSOR(RATIO(ADD(dlc, SUB(DELTA(SUB(act, che), 1), DELTA(SUB(SUB(lct, dlc), txp), 1))), lt), 1)
evaluated.hypothesis: What matters for refinancing is what fraction of a firm's whole obligation stack must be funded within the year, and that fraction includes not only debt maturing but the cash the firm has already committed to unfunded receivables and inventory; a firm with a long-dated liability structure can carry accruals that would sink a firm whose claims are front-loaded.
evaluated.reasoning: This is a maturity-structure measure rather than a shortfall measure — the two themes are combined inside a single fraction whose numerator is near-term cash claims from both accrual commitments and debt, and whose denominator is the entire liability stack — so it is neither a funding gap nor a coverage ratio and carries no cash-earnings or margin term at all. That absence is the point: it is the one construct in the family that cannot be confounded with the profitability anomaly, which has been an open objection to every sales-deflated version.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Free Cash Flow Coverage Of Interest Bearing Debt
evaluated.expression: WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(ADD(pi, dp), SUB(DELTA(SUB(act, che), 1), DELTA(SUB(SUB(lct, dlc), txp), 1))), ADD(dlc, dltt)), 1)
evaluated.hypothesis: The single number a credit analyst computes is free cash flow to total debt — cash earnings less the working capital they were consumed by, against the borrowings that must eventually be repaid — and equity prices should reward this quantity most where accruals have quietly eroded it.
evaluated.reasoning: The archive's coverage constructs all deflate by current or non-long-term liabilities and include the cash stock in the numerator, making them liquidity ratios; this is a pure flow-to-total-debt solvency multiple, a different economic quantity that ranks a cash-poor but strongly converting firm above a cash-rich but absorbing one. It keeps the accrual measure first-order in the numerator — net working-capital absorption is directly subtracted from cash earnings — so earnings quality drives the ratio rather than sitting as a second-order adjustment.
evaluated.author: proposer

considered.name: Accruals Under Liquidity Squeeze
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(SUB(ib, oancf), at)), RANK(RATIO(lct, act)))
considered.hypothesis: Accrual-based earnings are least credible when current liabilities crowd out current assets, because near-term liquidity pressure motivates receivable/inventory stretching and delays in payable settlement.
considered.reasoning: The second leg is the inverted current ratio, a classic short-horizon distress gauge distinct from long-run leverage, so this isolates liquidity-driven rather than solvency-driven accrual risk. Firms scoring high on both legs are booking non-cash earnings precisely when working capital must be converted to cash, making reversal and negative earnings surprises likely.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Accruals When Retained Earnings Are Negative
considered.expression: MUL(RATIO(SUB(ib, oancf), at), INDICATOR(NEG(RATIO(re, at)), 0))
considered.hypothesis: For firms with a cumulative deficit (negative retained earnings), reported accruals carry almost no information about sustainable profitability and largely reflect survival-motivated earnings management; the accrual anomaly should be switched on only in this fragile subset.
considered.reasoning: The indicator turns the accrual measure on only for firms whose accumulated losses signal distress, and sets it to zero for cumulatively profitable firms, so any predictive slope is attributable to the interaction and not to the standalone accrual effect. Deficit firms face equity-issuance and covenant thresholds that reward inflated accruals, which subsequently reverse.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Working Capital Accruals For Fragile Balance Sheets
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1), at)), RANK(SUMRANK(RATIO(lt, at), NEG(RATIO(re, at)))))
considered.hypothesis: Non-cash working capital build-ups (receivables and inventory growth net of operating payables) are a discretionary accrual channel whose reversal risk rises with a composite distress state combining high leverage and weak accumulated profitability.
considered.reasoning: Using the explicit working-capital accrual rather than the ib-minus-oancf gap isolates the balance-sheet channel most exposed to manipulation and write-downs. The distress leg is a two-variable SUMRANK so the conditioning state reflects both stock leverage and cumulative earnings deficit, making the interaction more robust than a single leverage cut.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Unstable Accruals In Weak Firms
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(VOL(RATIO(SUB(ib, oancf), at), 5)), RANK(NEG(RATIO(re, at))))
considered.hypothesis: Accrual quality is better measured by the instability of the accrual process than by its level: firms whose accruals swing violently have low earnings informativeness, and this opacity is priced most harshly, with a delay, when the firm is also financially fragile.
considered.reasoning: VOL over five years captures accrual-quality (information risk) rather than a one-period accrual level, giving a mechanism genuinely distinct from the classic accrual anomaly. Combined with a cumulative-deficit distress rank, it identifies opaque fragile firms where investors under-react to deteriorating fundamentals until losses are realized.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Accrual Slope Steepened By Rollover Risk
considered.expression: MUL(ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(ib, oancf), at), 1)), RANK(SUMRANK(RATIO(lt, at), RATIO(dlc, ADD(dlc, dltt)))))
considered.hypothesis: Distress does not add to the accrual effect, it steepens it: the price of an extra dollar of non-cash earnings should become more negative as a firm's debt burden and near-term rollover needs rise, while cash-backed (low-accrual) earnings should be rewarded most at exactly those same levered firms because they demonstrate genuine debt-service capacity.
considered.reasoning: Centering the accrual leg with ZSCORE makes the signal exactly zero for a median-accrual firm regardless of its distress rank, so the distress leg contributes no standalone level effect and only modulates the slope on accruals — this is the interaction term itself rather than an additive blend of two known predictors. The distress rank combines stock leverage with the short-term share of debt, capturing refinancing pressure that both motivates earnings management and prevents the firm from absorbing the accrual reversal.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Accrual Gap Per Dollar Of Liquidity Buffer
considered.expression: WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(ib, oancf), MAX(wcap, che)), 1)
considered.hypothesis: What matters is the size of the unbacked earnings claim relative to the liquidity cushion available to absorb its reversal; deflating the accrual gap by the buffer (the larger of net working capital or cash) mechanically magnifies the measure for thin-buffer, liquidity-constrained firms and shrinks it for cash-rich firms, so distress enters with the economically correct direction.
considered.reasoning: This fixes the earlier deflator inversion: the denominator is a distress-decreasing quantity, so the same dollar of accruals receives a much larger negative weight for fragile firms than for liquid ones. Flooring the buffer at cash keeps the deflator positive and interpretable for firms with negative working capital, and 1% winsorization controls the small-denominator tail while retaining broad coverage.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Receivable Inventory Build Under Leverage
considered.expression: MUL(ZSCORE(WINSOR(NEG(RATIO(ADD(recch, invch), at)), 1)), RANK(RATIO(lt, at)))
considered.hypothesis: The accrual channel most exposed to manipulation is the build-up of receivables and inventory reported directly in the cash-flow statement; the market should penalize an extra dollar of such non-cash earnings much more steeply when the firm carries a heavy liability burden that it cannot service with paper profits.
considered.reasoning: Cash-flow-statement components (recch, invch enter with decrease-positive sign, hence NEG) give a cleaner accrual measure than the balance-sheet difference and avoid the merger/acquisition contamination in DELTA-based working capital. Centering the accrual leg with ZSCORE means a median-accrual firm scores zero at every leverage level, so the leverage rank only steepens the accrual slope rather than adding a standalone distress tilt.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Depreciation Shading By Levered Firms
considered.expression: MUL(ZSCORE(WINSOR(NEG(DELTA(RATIO(dp, sale), 1)), 1)), RANK(RATIO(lt, at)))
considered.hypothesis: Extending asset lives or slowing write-offs lowers the depreciation-to-sales rate and inflates reported earnings without any cash consequence; this discretionary lever is most likely to be pulled, and most likely to precede impairments, at highly levered firms defending covenants.
considered.reasoning: Depreciation is a non-current accrual and an entirely different manipulation channel from working-capital accruals, so it tests whether the distress interaction generalizes beyond receivables and inventory. The ZSCORE-centered change ensures the leverage rank modulates the slope on depreciation shading rather than contributing a standalone leverage effect.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Payables Stretch Sign Flip
considered.expression: MUL(ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(apalch, at), 1)), ZSCORE(WINSOR(NEG(RATIO(re, at)), 1)))
considered.hypothesis: The payables component of accruals changes economic meaning with financial condition: for healthy firms a shrinking payables balance is a classic positive accrual that predicts poor returns, while for firms with an accumulated earnings deficit a swelling payables balance is involuntary supplier financing that precedes credit tightening and negative news.
considered.reasoning: Both legs are now demeaned, so the product is the pure interaction term and carries no standalone loading on the low-retained-earnings distress effect the critic identified. The sign convention is internally coherent precisely because apalch enters cash flow with the opposite sign to an accrual: the (low apalch, healthy) quadrant is the high-accrual Sloan case and the (high apalch, deficit) quadrant is the supplier-stretch case, and both are predicted to underperform.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Cumulative Accrual Overhang In Chronically Weak Firms
considered.expression: MUL(ZSCORE(WINSOR(TS_SUM(NEG(RATIO(ADD(recch, invch), at)), 3), 1)), RANK(NEG(MA(RATIO(pi, at), 3))))
considered.hypothesis: A single year of working-capital accruals is noisy, but three consecutive years of unreversed receivable and inventory build create an overhang of soft assets whose eventual write-down is most damaging for firms with chronically weak pretax profitability, which lack the earnings cushion to absorb it.

The accrual leg is demeaned so the distress leg only steepens the accrual slope, and the multi-year accumulation plus multi-year profitability state is a distinguishable reversal-timing hypothesis rather than the documented one-year loss-firm accrual result.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Opaque Other Accruals In Fragile Firms
considered.expression: MUL(ZSCORE(WINSOR(ABS(RATIO(aoloch, at)), 1)), RANK(SUMRANK(RATIO(lt, at), NEG(RATIO(re, at)))))

The opacity leg is demeaned so the ranked distress composite modulates the opacity slope instead of reintroducing the standalone distress return effect.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Illiquid Accrual Mix Under Leverage
considered.expression: MUL(ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(recch, invch), at), 1)), RANK(RATIO(lt, at)))
considered.hypothesis: Holding total working-capital accruals roughly fixed, their composition matters for levered firms: inventory build is illiquid, obsolescence-prone and poor collateral, whereas receivables can be factored or securitized, so a mix tilted toward inventory accruals is far more dangerous when debt must be serviced.

Demeaning the composition leg leaves the leverage rank acting purely as a slope modulator, and the hypothesis is a collateral-liquidity mechanism that neither accrual level nor leverage identifies alone.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Accruals While Leverage Is Rising
considered.expression: MUL(ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(DELTA(ADD(SUB(wcap, che), dlc), 1), dp), at), 1)), RANK(DELTA(RATIO(lt, at), 1)))
considered.hypothesis: Distress is a trajectory, not just a level: soft accrual-based earnings reported in the same year that the liability-to-asset ratio is climbing indicate a firm funding working-capital expansion with new debt, and it is this dynamic combination — not static leverage — that precedes forced reversal and write-downs.

Stable high-leverage utilities and REITs, which contaminate level-based conditioning, receive no weight here unless their balance sheets are actually worsening.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Accruals Against Rollover Pressure
considered.expression: MUL(ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(DELTA(ADD(SUB(wcap, che), dlc), 1), dp), at), 1)), RANK(RATIO(dlc, lt)))
considered.hypothesis: What makes accruals dangerous is near-term cash need rather than total indebtedness: a firm whose debt is concentrated in current maturities must convert receivables and inventory into cash within months, so accrual-heavy earnings at such firms are the least likely to survive contact with the refinancing calendar.

It also matches the economic story's emphasis on liquidity pressure rather than solvency.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Debt Financed Accrual Build
considered.expression: MIN(ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(DELTA(ADD(SUB(wcap, che), dlc), 1), dp), at), 1)), ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(DELTA(ADD(dlc, dltt), 1), at), 1)))
considered.hypothesis: The dangerous case is not accruals as such but accruals that had to be funded externally: a firm whose receivables and inventory swell while it simultaneously raises new short- and long-term debt is converting borrowed cash into soft assets, and that combination precedes both accrual reversal and rising default risk.

The short leg is symmetric and economically clean: firms generating cash while retiring debt, which is the survivorship profile the accrual-distress story predicts should outperform.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Low Depreciation Rate Versus Peers Under Leverage
considered.expression: MUL(IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(NEG(RATIO(dp, LAG(at, 1))), 1)), RANK(RATIO(lt, at)))
considered.hypothesis: Within an industry, a firm charging unusually little depreciation against its beginning-of-year asset base is assuming longer useful lives and understating the cost of capacity, inflating current earnings; levered firms have the covenant incentive to make that choice and the highest subsequent impairment risk.
considered.reasoning: Replacing the growth difference with an industry-demeaned level removes the direct loading on asset growth that made the previous version a proxy for the investment anomaly already spanned by CMA, and deflating by lagged assets means current-year capital spending does not mechanically depress the ratio. Putting dp in the numerator rather than in a growth rate also eliminates the instability for small-depreciation firms that the critic flagged.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Accrual Spike Against Own History In Fragile Firms
considered.expression: MUL(ZSCORE(TS_RANK(RATIO(SUB(DELTA(ADD(SUB(wcap, che), dlc), 1), dp), at), 5)), RANK(SUMRANK(RATIO(lt, at), NEG(RATIO(re, at)))))
considered.hypothesis: An accrual that is extreme relative to the firm's own five-year history is a far stronger manipulation flag than an accrual that is merely large in the cross-section, because it controls for the firm's stable business model; such a self-referential spike should be most reversal-prone at firms with high leverage and accumulated deficits.

TS_RANK measures position in the firm's own distribution instead of volatility, which sidesteps the contested accrual-quality risk premium and produces a bounded, outlier-resistant accrual leg that is demeaned before the distress rank modulates its slope.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Accrual Build Per Dollar Of Equity Cushion
considered.expression: WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(DELTA(ADD(SUB(wcap, che), dlc), 1), dp), MAX(ceq, che)), 1)
considered.hypothesis: The economically relevant scale for an accrual is the loss-absorbing capital that must absorb its reversal, not total assets: the same dollar of soft working-capital growth is trivial for a firm with a thick book equity cushion and existential for a thinly capitalized one, so deflating by the cushion embeds distress directly in the measurement.

Flooring the denominator at cash keeps it positive for near-zero or negative book equity firms, and 1% winsorization controls the thin-cushion tail while retaining the broad coverage of balance-sheet inputs.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Accruals Against Cash Adjusted Rollover Pressure
considered.expression: MUL(ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(DELTA(ADD(SUB(wcap, che), dlc), 1), dp), at), 1)), RANK(SUMRANK(RATIO(dlc, lt), NEG(RATIO(che, lct)))))
considered.hypothesis: Rollover pressure only bites when the firm cannot self-fund the maturing claim, so the conditioning state should combine a short-maturity debt structure with a thin cash buffer relative to current obligations; accruals booked by firms scoring high on both are the least likely to survive the refinancing calendar.

considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Soft Asset Build Under Rollover Pressure
considered.expression: MUL(ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(DELTA(SUB(act, che), 1), dp), at), 1)), RANK(RATIO(dlc, lt)))
considered.hypothesis: The reversal-prone element of accruals is the growth of non-cash current assets — receivables and inventory the firm must eventually convert to cash — and it is this asset-side softness, not the working-capital netting of liabilities, that becomes dangerous when debt is maturing.

If the effect survives, the mechanism is genuinely about soft assets meeting short-dated liabilities rather than about debt appearing twice.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Soft Assets Funded By Maturing Debt
considered.expression: MIN(ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(DELTA(SUB(act, che), 1), dp), at), 1)), ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(DELTA(dlc, 1), lt), 1)))
considered.hypothesis: A firm that expands receivables and inventory while simultaneously increasing its short-dated borrowings has created an explicit maturity mismatch — illiquid soft assets financed by claims that come due within a year — and this specific funding pattern, not accruals or borrowing alone, forecasts distress-driven underperformance.

considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Operating Liability Stretch Under Rollover Pressure
considered.expression: MUL(ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(DELTA(SUB(SUB(lct, dlc), txp), 1), at), 1)), RANK(RATIO(dlc, lt)))
considered.hypothesis: A rapid build in non-debt, non-tax current liabilities — trade payables and accrued expenses — is conventionally a negative accrual and good news, but for firms already facing maturing debt it is involuntary financing from suppliers and employees that precedes credit withdrawal and operating disruption.
considered.reasoning: This revives the payables sign-flip idea whose generation-1 test pointed the right way (FF5 t = −1.69) but was crippled by 6% coverage from cash-flow-statement data, rebuilding it from balance-sheet current liabilities net of debt and taxes. considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Three Year Soft Asset Overhang Meets Refinancing
considered.expression: MUL(ZSCORE(WINSOR(TS_SUM(RATIO(SUB(DELTA(SUB(act, che), 1), dp), at), 3), 1)), RANK(SUMRANK(RATIO(dlc, lt), NEG(RATIO(che, lct)))))
considered.hypothesis: What must be liquidated when debt comes due is the accumulated stock of soft assets, not a single year's flow; three years of uninterrupted, undepreciated working-capital build creates an overhang whose forced unwinding is triggered precisely when short-dated debt and a thin cash buffer force the firm to raise cash from its balance sheet.
